name: Choice Overload
description: Beyond a certain point, more options reduce rather than increase the likelihood of choosing at all, and reduce satisfaction with whatever is chosen.
design_relevance_note: Frequently cited as blanket justification for minimizing options in any interface — the actual evidence is real but much more conditional and contested than the popular framing suggests.
myth_risk_note: Choice overload shows genuine empirical backing via meta-analyses, but the effect is highly context-dependent and the literature has publication bias. Scheibehenne's (2010) finding of near-zero mean effect size and Simonsohn's p-curve analysis showing inflated effects suggest the phenomenon is much weaker and more conditional than popularly portrayed, creating moderate zombie-fact risk despite some rigorous backing.
prevalence_note: Extremely widely taught and cited in UX practice, largely due to Schwartz's popular book — one of the most mainstream 'design laws' in this taxonomy despite the underlying science being contested.

findings.description: Across 63 conditions from 50 experiments (N = 5,036), the overall effect of choice overload on consumer motivation/satisfaction was virtually zero on average, with considerable heterogeneity between studies — moderators (e.g. decision difficulty, complexity, prior preferences) determine whether an overload effect appears at all, contradicting a simple 'more options always worse' generalization.
findings.source_title: Can There Ever Be Too Many Options? A Meta-Analytic Review of Choice Overload

findings.description: Shoppers/participants offered a limited set of options (~6) were more likely to purchase and reported greater satisfaction with their choice than those offered an extensive set (~24-30) — the original empirical basis for the 'choice overload' claim.
findings.source_title: When Choice Is Demotivating: Can One Desire Too Much of a Good Thing?
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: The jam study: a smaller selection of jams outsold a larger one 10-to-1
applications.description: Iyengar & Lepper set up tasting displays of gourmet jams in a real upscale grocery store, alternating between a small selection (6 varieties) and a large one (24 varieties). The large display attracted more browsers, but only 3% of those who tasted from it went on to buy a jar, versus 30% of those who tasted from the small display -- ten times the purchase rate from a smaller selection.
applications.ethical_note: The single most-cited real-world demonstration of choice overload, run in an actual store rather than a lab -- but the same Freakonomics source honestly reports a serious complication: psychologist Benjamin Scheibehenne's attempts to directly replicate the jam study (and a similar luxury-chocolate version) found no sign of the effect at all, and a meta-analysis pooling published and unpublished studies of choice overload broadly found 'no important difference either way' on average, with Scheibehenne himself concluding 'if you did one of these studies tomorrow, the most probable result would be no effect.' This entry is kept as the field's canonical illustration of the concept, but should never be cited as if the underlying phenomenon were a settled, reliable law -- it is genuinely contested.

applications.title: YouTube's 'Something Different' section failing to relieve choice overload
applications.description: YouTube introduced a 'Something Different' section intended to break users out of repetitive recommendation loops, but the section continued surfacing similar content (the same creators and topics) rather than genuinely different options -- presented as a case where more perceived choice didn't actually reduce the paralysis it was meant to solve.
applications.ethical_note: Framed by the source as a design shortcoming rather than intentional manipulation, but worth naming the incentive question directly: a recommendation feature that fails to deliver genuine variety happens to also keep users inside familiar, engagement-optimized content longer -- there's no evidence in the source that this was deliberate, but the alignment between the flaw and the platform's own engagement incentive is worth flagging rather than assuming pure accident.
